MR. HERRIDGE    ALLEGED IMPROPER USE OF HOUSE OF COMMONS STATIONERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege on information supplied to me by a highly indignant editor of a daily newspaper that supports the present government. It is a question that should concern all members of this house, namely the improper use of House of Commons stationery.
There is in Ottawa a cartoonist named Mr. Gordon Johnston, who makes his headquarters at 162 Belmont Avenue. Mr. Johnston is the creator of a dubious new comic strip entitled "Jeff Buchanon, parliamentary press gallery reporter". Last week Mr. Johnston and his associates distributed to the newspapers across Canada the details of their comic strip service. The fabulous Buchanon, they say-
-is going to work on comic pages across Canada on May 16. If you want him on staff, exclusive in your area, send me a wire, collect.
Mr. Johnston and his group are apparently a well financed free enterprise organization. It can afford to print and send out to prospective newspaper customers masses of letters and advertising material, and apparently to pay its postage bills and accept collect telegrams. But evidently it cannot afford to pay for its own envelopes.
This advertising propaganda arrived on the desks of newspaper editors across Canada in official House of Commons envelopes bearing the crown and the Canadian royal coat of arms. My point of privilege is that this is a highly improper use of House of Commons stationery.
I wish to bring to the attention of the house the fact that this advertisement, which reads:
The parliament of Canada in the spotlight with Jeff Buchanon of the parliamentary press gallery-
I have never heard of him-
-a man, around "the House'.
-contains an etching of the House of Commons and the figure of the mythical Jeff Buchanon, who somewhat resembles a picture of Mr. Arthur Blakely, taken some ten years ago.
Mr. Speaker, while I cannot raise a question of privilege concerning individual members of the press gallery, I must remind the house that on one occasion Sir Winston Churchill said that the press gallery as an institution is an emanation of a free parliament whose members have somewhat more intimate relations with the members of the House of Commons than other groups. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I bring to the attention of the house the fact that this advertizing does convey the false impression that the material in question, the reporting and the cartoons to follow, emanate from the parliamentary press gallery.
While I cannot raise this as a direct question of privilege, with our knowledge of the rectitude and propriety of the gentlemen concerned and the extent to which they cherish their privileges and relationships in this house, I know this aspect of the question will concern all members of the house and should therefore receive their consideration.
This being an improper use of House of Commons stationery and, as a consequence, a violation of our statutes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That the subject matter of my question of privilege be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for its investigation and later report to the house.

subtopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope you will not rule me out of order if under motions I express the warm welcome of the official opposition to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) on his return to the house after what was, I know, a very arduous as well as a very important mission. We are delighted to see him looking so well; arduous missions seem to have that effect on him. Perhaps while I am on my feet I might venture to suggest to the Prime Minister that he should make a report to the house at this time on his mission abroad.

subtopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should just like a moment in which to associate the C.C.F. group with the words of the Leader of the Opposition in welcoming the Prime Minister on his return to Canada after having taken part in this very important commonwealth prime ministers' conference.
Those of us who have known the Prime Minister for many, many years realize that he is an excellent traveller, and that experiences which might fatigue the average man seem to be taken by the Prime Minister in his stride. I think the right hon. gentleman thrives on this kind of arduous work. We are sincerely pleased to see him back in such good health.

These occasions, for some reason or another, do not entirely coincide with my efforts to maintain my weight at a reasonable level. I think that is one of the difficulties I have; attending meetings such as this has, for me, a rather challenging effect, and one of these times I am going to call in the hon. member for Essex East to give me some ideas in connection with this very difficult problem that I face.

subtopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN
speechtext:
I would think that calling the hon. member in on so weighty a problem it might be sufficient, but it may be that there will be other occasions in future.
At this time, having expressed my thanks and very deep appreciation for the attitude taken by both hon. gentlemen who have spoken and by the house in general, may I begin by referring to the communiques which were issued. They have been analysed at length, and I propose to ask the leave of the house, in accordance with past experience in this regard, to have the first communique of May 3 and the final communique at the termination of the conference printed as an appendix to Hansard.
However, even in following this course it is necessary for me to elaborate to some extent upon the main trends and, as I see them, the achievements of the meeting. I came back from the London conference feeling that, bearing in mind the difficult circumstances arising from the situation in South Africa, the conference was generally useful and successful.
Many observers have, of course, pointed out that the proceedings of the meetings did not result in any perceptible change in the attitude of the South African government. It was not to be expected, however, that magic improvements could take place in a situation of such tension and complexity. I believe that those who in future will examine and judge this period in commonwealth history will decide that this meeting did not fail to respond to the stern test to which it was put.

I would be the last to say that everything was achieved that I would have desired.
I do not contend that in so far as the communique is concerned it can convey the full nature and substance of the deliberations that took place. On occasions in the past I have heard my predecessors, Right Hon. Mackenzie King and Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, report on conferences they had attended. In every case it was made perfectly clear that while no decisions were made or can be made in these informal circumstances, there is a oneness of mind that comes about through the exchange of ideas.
There was no disposition on the part of any of the representatives to evade this issue, and there was no lack of frankness in private and informal discussions. I underline the fact that, as the Leader of the Opposition knows very well from his own experience, only in unanimity can there be a final communique issued. Everything that is included therein represents the agreement of all. To bring together the representatives of one quarter of the world's population, belonging to many races and being of many colours, I think it is quite an unusual result that several conclusions were arrived at unanimously which cannot but result in the possibility of change along the lines generally desired.
Despite the profound differences which prevailed and persisted throughout, it was possible for a communique to be issued. This was difficult with two inherently conflicting elements to be reconciled. First, it had become essential that a way be found for commonwealth governments to make clear their intentions on this central question of racial relations. Second, it was desirable that this should be done without violation of the traditional practice of these meetings that the internal affairs of member countries are not the subject of formal discussion. I believe now more certainly than I did when I spoke here on April 27 that any departure from this last principle would mean the end of the commonwealth as we know it; because if we ever arrive at the point where we will discuss the internal affairs of other countries and determine the course by a majority, then there will be problems that will arise and it could only mean that several countries in the commonwealth could not accept the decisions of the majority. I need not go into particulars in that regard; I think a number would come to mind immediately, including the question of migration.
Personally, as the house knows, I was of those who thought it worth while to try
Report on Commonwealth Conference to achieve the first objective of enabling the views of prime ministers to be expressed without sacrificing the principle of noninterference, which is one of the elements of the commonwealth association. I took the view that notwithstanding the depth of feeling on this racial issue-my views throughout the years and now are a matter of record -I believed it would be wrong and damaging to the spirit and fabric of the commonwealth partnership if a majority of the commonwealth governments, finding themselves allied in condemnation of one or more of their number, were to constitute themselves as a court of judgment. I saw, as I said a moment ago, in that trend an end of the association as we know it. The seed of mutual recrimination would threaten the partnership whose essence has always been tolerance, restraint and free co-operation.
I wish that hon. members could have been there. Strong feelings were held in the informal meetings. Men like the president of Pakistan, the prime ministers of India, of Malaya and of Ghana accepted this view as essential to the preservation and maintenance of our relationship. There was unanimous acceptance of the principle that internal affairs of free states are not to be the subject of formal discussion, and that any action in that regard would damage the strength and ultimately the preservation of the institution itself.
I cannot reveal, as hon. members know, in the tradition of those meetings, the substance of the talks. They were at times bilateral, at times in small groups, and at other times all the representatives took part in an informal and private exchange of views. For my part, I had two lengthy and private personal conversations with Mr. Louw; I participated in other informal discussions. I left Mr. Louw in no doubt that in Canada there is no sympathy for policies of racial discrimination, on whatever grounds they may be explained, and that such policies are basically incompatible with the multiracial nature of the commonwealth association. I made it clear to him that the policy of South Africa was a denial of the principle that human dignity and the worth of the individual, whatever his race and colour, must be respected, and that there could be no doubt as to our views in that connection. Indeed, those views are being generally expressed now.
A few weeks ago there were those who felt that what we required was condemnation by various parliaments. I think the events during the days of the conference were an answer to that contention. Our views, the views of all of us in other parts of the commonwealth, or most of the people in
3900	HOUSE OF
Report on Commonwealth Conference other parts of the commonwealth, were set out only a few days ago by the Archbishop of Canterbury when he said:
But the tragedy is that so far they (South Africa) have seemed to pay little or no regard to the burdens they are imposing on the hearts and consciences and political principles of those who are their brethren in the commonwealth, in culture, in Christian faith and in common humanity.
Only in the last 24 hours I have received from the Primate of the Anglican church of Canada the declaration of that church, which represents the views expressed at the 1958 Lambeth conference:
The conference affirms its belief in the natural dignity and value of every man of whatever colour or race as created in the image of God. In the light of this belief the conference affirms that neither race nor colour is in itself a barrier to any aspect of that life in family and community for which God created all men. It therefore condemns discrimination of any kind on the grounds of race or colour alone.
I would be less than frank if I did not say that I cannot report that there was any indication in Mr. Louw's attitude, representing his government, that he was moved by the arguments or concerned about the force of international opinion. However, he learned the viewpoint, he recognized that of all those present there no one, in the informal meetings or elsewhere, could give support to racial discrimination in a multiracial commonwealth.
It is clear that the issue of racial conflict will continue to pose a fundamental problem for commonwealth countries and, indeed, for the world community. My hope is that by this meeting we have assisted in the process of change. The matter was not on the agenda but it was discussed with clarity and frankness; and above all, by those from whom you would have expected the expression of violent opinions, with a dignity, a restraint and a recognition of the tremendous issues at stake that must give heart to all of us as to the meaning of the commonwealth as such.
International concern has been demonstrated in the United Nations. In the last few days the secretary general, Mr. Hammar-skjold, has been holding talks in London with Mr. Louw. Whatever the results may be, I am sure they will be aided in their talks by what took place at the conference. I hope the people of South Africa can work their way out of the dreadful impasse to which they have been brought. I hope their isolation on the continent of Africa will give them thought and a realization of the situation. It was a great South African, Field Marshal Smuts as he subsequently was, who as long ago as December, 1918, reminded us of this fact:


There is no doubt that mankind is once more on the move. The very foundations have been shaken and loosened and things are again fluid. The tents have been struck and the great caravan of humanity is once more on the march.
He was pointing to the need of new institutions, new ways of thought, new kinds of international behaviour if the world was to avoid the catastrophe of another war. His words were of prophetic application to his own continent.
It was made very clear in the communique that racial equality was of the essence. The communique had this to say:
Whilst reaffirming the traditional practice that commonwealth conferences do not discuss the internal affairs of member countries, ministers availed themselves of Mr. Louw's presence in London to have informal discussions with him about the racial situation in South Africa. During the informal discussions Mr. Louw gave information and answered questions on the union's policies, and the other ministers conveyed to him their views on the South African problem. The ministers emphasized that the commonwealth itself is a multiracial association and expressed the need to ensure good relations between all member states and peoples of the commonwealth.
We know the results of the assertion of racial superiority only a few years ago and the effects that followed from it. It is my hope that the South African government will heed and heed quickly the appeal that was made to it, not only in the communique but in personal conversations.
The government there has been planning to hold a referendum on the question of changing the present status of South Africa from a monarchy to that of a republic. In that regard it was pointed out that the choice between a monarchy and a republic is entirely the responsibility of the nation concerned. Then there are these significant words. I am not going to interpret them, because they require no interpretation; their significance lies in the fact that they were accepted unanimously by all who were there.
In the event of South Africa deciding to become a republic and if the desire was subsequently expressed to remain a number of the commonwealth, the meeting suggested that the South African government should then ask for the consent of the other commonwealth governments either at a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers or, if this were not practicable, by correspondence.
This established clearly that membership in the commonwealth is not a formality. These words speak for themselves. They make clear that the prime ministers were not prepared to give an advance assurance that South Africa might remain a member of the commonwealth in the event that a decision was made to adopt the status of a republic. Therefore the important point is that if a change of status does take place as

a result of the referendum, the consent of the other commonwealth governments will be required as a pre-condition of continued membership. Again I emphasize the fact that this was accepted by all.
The attention given to the South African problem, however, should not be allowed to obscure the deliberation which took place on many other subjects. The nature of those deliberations is fairly reflected in the communique, but I am going to make a few general references thereto. The multiracial nature of the commonwealth was underlined by the admission of Ghana three years ago at the last meeting, by the participation of the prime minister of Malaya this year and by the fact that the federation of Nigeria, with a population of 35 million, will join the family on the 1st of October and that Sierra Leone and other countries of various colours and races will, it is expected, soon be applying for membership.
What has taken place here is a recognition that there is no automatic membership in the commonwealth, and I believe it is also suggestive of the possibility that the time is not far distant when acceptance by custom rather than by declaration of	certain basic	principles, including
equality of all races, colours and creeds, will be assured. This view is underlined in various editorials to which I could refer. I draw the attention of the house to the fact that Canada's views were known, but the fact that we had not had a resolution placed Canada's representative in a position to speak to Mr. Louw in a way that did not arouse his antagonism. What happened here is well set out in the London Financial Times:
If the South African government carries through its plan for making the country into a republic ...
important constitutional matters will arise. It goes on to say:
More important even than these constitutional considerations is the simple truth expressed by Mr. Diefenbaker last week that a commonwealth in which the majority of the population is coloured must unequivocally accept racial equality.
The seriousness of racial problems varies widely from member country to member country. Not all of them have an untarnished record. Yet the position today is that the truth of Mr. Diefenbaker's proposition is accepted in theory at least everywhere in the western world except in South Africa. Refusal to accept it would mean losing the struggle against communism by default.
And so I might go on in that regard. This was an important step forward, and in that connection it is important internationally. We reviewed the international political situation. As to our views on the summit conference, I shall not now refer to them in view of what has taken place today.
Report on Commonwealth Conference
There was universal agreement on the importance of developing a general detente in international relations, the urgent need of concluding a broad agreement to end the testing of nuclear weapons, and the desirability of finding avenues of progress in the field of general disarmament. There was an awareness of the growing importance of China in world affairs; and in particular, in order to ensure the implementation of any international agreement on disarmament, the participation of China was recognized as being of first importance.
The meeting was notable also for the growing recognition it gave to the development of the economic needs of the newly independent countries of Africa. I have mentioned already the fact that Nigeria will become a member. I have also referred to the second constitutional decision which arose from the intention of Ghana to introduce a republican form of constitution by July 1. In connection with the decision regarding Ghana's relation to the commonwealth, the government of Ghana applied to continue as a member, thus again illustrating the flexible nature of the commonwealth relationship which permits member countries to remain in free association despite the differences in their forms of government.
As to the economic needs of the emerging nations of Africa, there was a unanimous recognition that a substantial expansion of economic assistance was necessary in order to assist these countries to achieve selfsustaining growth. The greatest remaining underdeveloped region of the world is Africa, where no special international economic assistance program has been established and were the flow of investment and aid funds, in comparison with that to other underdeveloped countries, is disproportionately small. The Prime Minister of Ghana is seriously concerned about this situation. It was agreed that unless measures are quickly taken in this crucial formative period in the history of these new African nations there may very well develop in those nations doubts as to the good will of the developed countries of the west, and they may be tempted to look for sympathy and assistance in other directions.
Mention was made of what the Colombo plan had done. There is no such type of international assistance as yet available in Africa. Consideration is therefore being given to the possibility of co-operative action among members of the commonwealth in assisting the economic development of countries in Africa which have recently attained or are approaching independence. This matter will be studied by the various commonwealth
3902	HOUSE OF
Report on Commonwealth Conference governments, and will be examined at the next meeting of the commonwealth economic consultative council in London.
On behalf of the government Canada indicated willingness, subject to parliament, to participate in such a program. I cannot at present, however, indicate the scope of the aid program which may flow from the decisions of the conference, or offer any forecast of what will be required from Canada.
Then in connection with the need for technical assistance for the newly independent countries of both Asia and Africa, the Prime Minister of Malaya drew attention to the fact that his government required the services of persons with specialized skills and experience in the administrative and technical fields. There was general agreement that everything should be done to foster and encourage exchanges of specialized personnel, and that the question should be taken into consideration by the commonwealth economic consultative council.
A further subject-and this was one that will become of increasing importance; it was mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in his remarks in April 

was the constitutional development of the commonwealth. Up to the present time it has been possible to preserve the intimate character of the prime ministers' meetings. The essence of these meetings is that they are conducted, as I said, in an informal way. No resolutions are moved; no votes are taken. Progress is made by agreement after discussion. However, as the membership of the commonwealth grows, new problems as to how these meetings will be conducted will arise.
One has only to note that at the present rate of accession to the commonwealth, within a very few years the present membership of 11 will be expanded to 16 or 18. How shall such a wide membership be reconciled with the maintenance of frank, intimate and profitable discussion? What about the size of the gathering? What about the size of the nations? There will be tremendous and fantastic disparities in population, importance and size, India with a population of 450 million and Sierra Leone with 2 million.
The various commonwealth governments will have to give consideration to such questions as membership, weight by population, the rotation of membership as in the security council, regional groupings of nations within the commonwealth, and representation of such groups. These are some of the problems which will have to receive consideration. I am not indicating any view with regard to them. These are some of the problems that will now have to be examined in the light


of the tremendous expansion that is taking place and the number of nations which are joining us.
To those who say there is nothing in the commonwealth relationship, may I say that it is of interest to note that in all the years the commonwealth has been in its present form only one nation which attained independence, namely Burma, did not apply for membership. In other words, these nations representing various colours have of their own volition decided to remain with the institution and become active and effective members.
Mr. Speaker, one other matter I want to refer to is the question of trade. Western Europe represents a very important market for all commonwealth countries. With the exception of the United Kingdom most of them, like Canada, are important suppliers to western Europe of agricultural products. It was therefore recognized that it would be a matter of much concern if our competitive access to these markets was impaired in any way by the agricultural policies which may be followed by the European economic community. This community can have a tremendous influence in the direction of world trade, and this is significant for the primary producing countries of the commonwealth. It was urged that both the Six and the Seven should pursue trade policies that are consistent with their obligations under GATT. In this way western Europe would be contributing to the general economic well-being of the world, and particularly of the underdeveloped countries.
Some concern was expressed about the possibility that the plans to create a successor organization for the O.E.E.C. might lead to exclusive or restrictive arrangements which would not take into account the interests of countries outside Europe. I explained that while Canada expected to be a full member of the revised organization, we attached great importance to ensuring that its efforts should be directed toward improving multilateral trading conditions and that we did not regard this as in any way an exclusive organization which would be harmful to the interests of other commonwealth members. I believe the members of the commonwealth share our concern that the economic division in western Europe should not lead or be permitted to lead to political division. It was also recognized, as I saw it, that the United Kingdom should continue to maintain the closest co-operation with the rest of the commonwealth in developing its own policies with regard to trade with western Europe.
Now, sir, to those who have predicted that the commonwealth was on a slippery slope,

I am convinced that it came out of the conference stronger than ever. It is impossible to convey to the members of this house the spirit that was apparent in the desire to assure the maintenance of unity without the sacrifice of principle on the part of any of the members. Each of the representatives, in a spirit of understanding, was conscious of and concerned with the welfare of all other members. While re-emphasizing the cardinal principle of the commonwealth, non-interference in domestic affairs, the multiracial nature and the need for recognition of equality of all races and peoples were recognized. In the informal meetings this was made clear and definite so that no one could misunderstand it.
I mentioned this earlier in another way, and I repeat it. While the commonwealth has no constitution, the membership and variety in population of the peoples that compose its membership demand the recognition of equality, and I believe the final communique made it clear that the recognition of these principles has been achieved in spirit.
As I return I am convinced of one thing. While there were those who were critical of the stand which was being taken, I think in the light of what has occurred the course followed was one that has assured the maintenance of the basic principles, and also made possible in the future the achievement of equality and the denial of discrimination. The ominous danger of commonwealth fission was prevented without the sacrifice of any vital principles by the prime ministers and representatives of the various countries. The course of reason, restraint and diplomacy was followed rather than that of judicial action. The various prime ministers who felt most strongly against fanatical racialism maintained a self control and a dignity in the presentation of their arguments which had its effect. I think it may be fairly said that an advance was made in the interracial and multiracial relationships of the many peoples of the commonwealth; and while collective action was asked by some before we met, it was asked by none by the time we separated.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think every member of the house will have listened with the greatest possible interest to the statement we have just heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), who represented
Report on Commonwealth Conference our country at this very important meeting of commonwealth prime ministers which, I think, had an importance which extended beyond the borders of the commonwealth itself.
The Prime Minister in his statement has indicated not only the far-reaching nature of the subjects under discussion but their complicated character as well. The formal results of the meeting are, as is customary in these cases, to be found in the communique issued by the prime ministers at the conclusion of the conference. But as the Prime Minister himself has indicated, a communique of this kind does not of course communicate everything that was done and said at the conference. A communique, especially a communique resulting from a conference of this kind within the commonwealth, has to be of a nature-always in the past it has been of a nature-which requires unanimous approval, and perhaps on this occasion there was some difficulty, as indeed there have been difficulties in the past, in securing that unanimous approval. In the very nature of things the communique represents, as it was bound to, the lowest common denominator of agreement.
I have no doubt, and the Prime Minister's remarks seemed to make it quite clear, that some of the more important discussions took place outside the formal meetings of the commonwealth prime ministers.
That has been the situation in the past. It has its advantages, but of course it could also have its dangers. I recall in the past that over the issue of Kashmir-a very different issue from that which divided the commonwealth conference on this occasion-it was not possible to have a discussion of that controversial matter inside the meeting; any discussion which took place had to be outside the formal agenda.
However, it is clear from the communique, from the report we have had from the Prime Minister, and from the reports we have read in the press, that this conference made clear as perhaps has not been made clear before, at least so dramatically, the nature of the new commonwealth; its great potential value as a bridge between races and peoples and countries and continents; also its new problems and, indeed, certain new dangers which threaten its existence in a more acute form, perhaps, than we have had to face in the commonwealth in the past, dangers and difficulties which every member of this house hopes will be removed. These dangers and these difficulties arise from that very multiracial character which, if it is not accepted by all members of the commonwealth, with
3904	HOUSE OF
Report on Commonwealth Conference all its complications, will constitute a great threat to the future of the commonwealth, just as the complete acceptance of this new character of the commonwealth could constitute its greatest value in the future.
So these matters have to be faced, even though they cannot always appear in the record of the meeting itself. There is a real danger of what may arise if we neglect to do so. The Prime Minister of India who, I am sure, played his customary constructive role in this conference, is reported in the press to have said:
The commonwealth is facing basic problems-and some people begin to doubt whether this commonwealth is not becoming too vague to be identified as anything at all.
I would hope that Mr. Nehru, at the end of the conference, would perhaps be more optimistic than he was in that statement as to the possible results.
There was also a very interesting editorial in the London Times of May 10. I have no doubt the Prime Minister has had it drawn to his attention. Dealing with this matter with all the impressive authority that goes with that historic newspaper, the Times had this to say:
The commonwealth is a voluntary association and sooner or later every voluntary association has to recognize that though every member's private life is his own concern, yet each is judged by the company he keeps, and the honour of all may be involved in the private behaviour of one.
The editorial concluded with these words, which are full of sober significance:
It is a multiracial commonwealth.
That phrase is, of course, used in the communique.
If the deliberations of the prime ministers end in complete disagreement on one of the greatest questions of the day it is far better to announce the fact. There are other great questions; if there is unity on these it can also be declared, and with the greater prospect of being believed. The consequences that flow from both agreements and disagreements can then be worked out.
Mr. Speaker, the disagreement which obviously existed within the membership of the conference-the Prime Minister has frankly indicated it and, of course, we knew there would be such disagreement-was not announced in the communique. I can understand the reason for this, and I am not suggesting it should have been announced in the communique. But it is just as well for us to go behind the words of the communique and face the fact that disagreement exists, because I do not think I am exaggerating when I say the commonwealth on this occasion did face a very real threat to its existence-a veritable storm, as it has been described. Indeed, the Montreal Gazette referring only this morning to this "veritable


storm"-that was the expression the editor used-stated in an editorial on this subject, that it-that is, the commonwealth-has neither surmounted that storm nor succumbed to it. Perhaps that is the fairest analysis that could be made in a few words with regard to the conference and, indeed, to the communique.
The conference certainly postponed a showdown-if I may use that expression-on the issue on which some of its members felt so strongly, the issue of race discrimination and the policy of apartheid in South Africa. I am not complaining about that, as long as the cost which had to be paid for that postponement was not too high, and I do not think in this instance it was. Perhaps the postponement of this issue at this time was the best course to take in London, providing the period which has been given for the reconsideration of this matter by the government of South Africa can be used for improving the situation in regard to this situation in that country.
The Prime Minister indicated today that he made it clear to the South African representatives where Canada and Canadians stand on this matter. I am glad he has done that. Indeed, the Prime Minister's intervention in this matter in this informal way does illustrate, in a sense, the dilemma he mentioned about intervention or non-intervention in commonwealth affairs. The situation we have reached now is that while there cannot be formal intervention in domestic matters at the conference table-that has been the tradition up to the present-there may, nevertheless, be informal intervention of the kind the Prime Minister has mentioned. I am glad the right hon. gentleman took advantage of the opportunity to make the attitude of Canada perfectly clear with regard to this policy.
The right hon. gentleman also said-and I think the record indicates that he was correct, at least the record that was made public -that unfortunately nothing has yet emerged which would indicate that there is any likelihood of the South African government modifying its position on this matter of principle which is so vital to us. Therefore we can only hope that the words which were uttered, the attitudes which were taken and the moderation which was shown at the prime ministers' conference on this occasion will have their effect in those places where change can be brought about.
However, we must be clear that the situation has been postponed only. Indeed, the Prime Minister made clear in reading from the communique that if and when South Africa decides, after an expression of the

opinion of its people, to become a republic, it will be required to apply for continuing membership in the commonwealth as a republic. No assurance has been given in advance in regard to any such request if and when it is made. I express the hope that if and when that time comes the situation in South Africa will be such that all members of the commonwealth will be happy to have South Africa continue its membership in this association.
The Montreal Star writing on this aspect of the matter on May 11 had this to say. I hope this is not too pessimistic, but in view of what the Prime Minister said it would not seem to be. The words of the editorial are:
They-
The members of the commonwealth.
-have sought to elicit some hint that South Africa might, some time and in some way, modify its apartheid policy.
They have got nowhere.
Let us hope that during this period between the meeting in London and the next meeting we will have got somewhere in connection with this matter.
The Prime Minister mentioned some other questions that came up at the commonwealth meeting. He dealt with the question of assistance to the new and emerging nations of Africa. I think all hon. members of the house are anxious as all Canadians are to do what we can to provide the kind of assistance needed, within the measure of our resources; not only material and economic assistance, but assistance through the sympathy and understanding we may show for the problems of these people, and assistance by the supply of technical and administrative personnel which in the early days of their existence is going to be, I am quite sure, their greatest problem.
The Prime Minister also mentioned that trade was discussed, and I am sure that was not the least important subject that came up for discussion at that conference. It is well that it should have come up at this particular time, because the European countries are trying to work out their own arrangements for economic co-operation leading, one might hope, one day to economic unity and who knows but to political unity. It is of the greatest possible importance that that be done not only without dividing Europe but also without dividing Europe from her friends across the Atlantic and inside the commonwealth.
There has been an important step made in that regard in recent weeks, at least in so far as a report is a step. If hon. members have read that report of the four O.E.E.C. representatives, as I have, they will I think
Report on Commonwealth Conference be struck by the fact that the recommendations in that report can be of very far-reaching significance indeed; because they lead inevitably to an association of the 19 European countries and the United States and Canada. They point the way toward that association, which in any event will take a long time to work out. But even 21 countries united on that basis will not be enough if other countries in the commonwealth who wish to come into that kind of lower tariff association are excluded. Therefore, perhaps, these matters as they were discussed in London may have had their own value in bringing about the widening of this kind of freer trade association.
The communique contains one sentence which I should like to read. The Prime Minister for very understandable reasons felt that at this time and in the present circumstances he would not deal with it in any detail. The sentence concerns a summit conference, and reads as follows:
They-
The members of the commonwealth.
-hoped that, on the basis of the preliminary work already done, the summit conference would be able to make some significant progress toward an eventual settlement, under international control, of the problem of disarmament.
Then they also expressed their general hope for success at this summit conference to which all men and women of good will throughout the world have been looking forward with hope not unmixed with anxiety. As reports have come over the wires this morning the anxiety is becoming a more powerful emotion than the hope, because so far as one can gather from the first meeting of the summit conference-and it is unwise to come to any premature conclusion on this matter-those hopes which were expressed by the commonwealth prime ministers may in the course of events be falsified.
I hope the leaders of the three western countries, the United States, the United Kingdom and France-and I am sure all hon. members of the house join me in this hope- will not accept the apparently brutal ultimatum submitted to the conference at its opening session by the leader of the Soviet union. This conference must not be allowed to break up in this way. Therefore if anything could be done, it should be done. If the commonwealth prime ministers were only meeting at this time collectively they might have been able to intervene collectively to prevent a break. Although I know this is perhaps going a little beyond the report of the commonwealth conference, but not very far-[DOT]

There is in this communique of the commonwealth conference a great deal-several paragraphs- devoted to the then forthcoming summit conference. All I would like to say on this occasion is that this conference must surely be kept going. The replies of the three western leaders to the statement of the Soviet leader this morning indicate that they are taking that view, too. I know the Canadian government will support them in that stand in any way it can.
I have one final suggestion to make, a very short one, before I sit down. My suggestion is that if the conference threatens to break up at once, even before it approaches the problems that are before it, then perhaps the secretary general of the United Nations, who is on that side of the world at this time, might ask that these four leaders meet with him to discuss ways and means of keeping the conference going.

subtopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER ON RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all listened with a great deal of attention to the statement made by the Prime Minister on returning to Canada from the commonwealth conference. Reference has been made by the Leader of the Opposition to the summit conference. I am not going to endeavour to make any detailed statement on the proceedings that are going on at the summit. We very fervently hope for all mankind that ideological differences may be bridged, that good will may assert itself, and that an agreement on disarmament in the interests of peace can be achieved as a result of the conference.
I would say that the leaders of the world should quit spying, quit threatening and quit stalling. Mankind is not interested at this time in threats or in any course that might be considered normal in normal circumstances. These are abnormal circumstances,


and the world is looking for abnormal action that will restore the confidence of mankind in its own survival.
I was encouraged by the general statement of the Prime Minister, and by the emphatic way he made the statement he gave to this house. As was mentioned by the Prime Minister, the second world war was fought to preserve the world from fascism, racial discrimination in its most ugly form. We trust that fascism and the appearance of fascism, no matter where it emerges, can be obliterated and that mankind will grant to one another complete racial equality.
I think the attitude of the Prime Minister confirmed the position taken by the C.C.F., namely that in an issue such as this it is essential for Canada to speak out strongly and with a united voice. I feel that as a result of the conference, and by the strength of the Prime Minister's statement today, he would have been in a better position when he went to the conference had he been armed with a unanimous vote of this House of Commons setting forth the Canadian point of view.
We trust that events as they unfold will see the relaxing of discrimination in South Africa. We are very much in favour of an expanding, of a growing and of a strengthened commonwealth, but we feel that to try to keep together at all costs this loose association of nations is not the best attitude or the objective that we should have. The commonwealth, to survive, must he based on solid principles, and one of those principles is the regard of man for his brother.
I think it should be made perfectly clear -the Prime Minister did not say it but I believe it is inherent in the statement he made-that if the people of South Africa by their vote should decide to become a republic and unless racial equality is restored Canada's attitude will be one of opposition to the admission of South Africa to the commonwealth as a republic. Any other attitude would be a denial of those important human principles.
The Prime Minister went on to refer to a number of other subjects, such as the desire for an end to nuclear testing, a review of the growing importance of China and the necessity of China coming into any general disarmament agreement. We suggest to the Prime Minister once again that now is the time for Canada to consider diplomatic recognition of China as a positive step toward bringing this nation into the councils of the world so that any disarmament agreement may be meaningful.
The Prime Minister dealt with a number of positive suggestions, including the one

that there should be a Colombo plan of assistance for the nations of Africa. This, we think, would be a very important step forward. We have been firm advocates of economic and technical assistance to emerging nations for many years. I now go on record once again as suggesting to the Canadian government that Canada should be prepared to use 1 per cent of its gross national product as the amount that would be suitable for our contribution to economic assistance to underdeveloped nations of the world.
The Prime Minister went on to deal with the importance of trade and the possible threat of the inner six and even the outer seven to commonwealth trade. I make the suggestion that now is the time for Canada to consider associating our nation with those other trading areas, and that we should be giving very close attention to plans directed toward the removal of trade barriers in this larger trading area and finally in other nations of the world.
The Prime Minister's statement, Mr. Speaker, I believe, shows that he has come back from this conference prepared to make a much stronger statement on the need for racial equality. We suggest to him various points that I have covered as ways and means of strengthening the commonwealth, of improving the lot of underdeveloped nations, and of playing our full part in the maintenance of world peace.

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I read the statement in the press. speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER POLICY, OPERATIONS AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
(1)	That a select committee be appointed to consider the policy, operations and expenditures of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon;
(2)	That nothwithstanding standing order 67, the committee shall consist of twenty members, of which eleven shall be a quorum;
(3)	That the committee be empowered to sit during the sittings of the house, to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee and to send for persons, papers and records.
He said; Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to dwell at great length on the subject of setting up this committee. The committee itself will have a great deal of work to do if it follows the course of the earlier committee of 1956, which assembled well over 400 pages of evidence. That makes it obvious that we cannot deal here, at the setting up of the committee, with all the matters which will come under its survey.
It has become customary for a select committee to look into the operations of nondepartmental government research organizations once during each parliament. The 1950
Atomic Energy Committee committee examined the operations of the national research council. At that time the council had responsibility for atomic energy in addition to its other functions. The 1956 committee examined the role of government in non-military research, including Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the national research council. The proposal now is that the present committee consider the policy, operations and expenditures of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. I should add that in 1956 Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited were under one head.
It is generally agreed that it is useful at intervals of four years or so to have a committee of the house examine the operations of the research organizations. The operations of a research organization are complex and require considerably more freedom and flexibility than is customary with other government operations. The technical complexity of the operations also makes it advisable for members in the house who are especially interested to obtain a more detailed knowledge of the operations of such organizations.
The Canadian research complex involves three parts; the universities, industry and government. The universities are the basis of the whole research structure, and there has been a very great development of university research in Canada over the past 40 years. In fact when the national research council was formed in 1917 its major activity was the development of scientific research in universities, and there is no question but that the present status of science in Canada is largely due to the support thus given by the national research council.
At the end of the first war there was little research in Canadian universities except in a few isolated instances. Largely because of national research council support a steady development occurred in the years from 192039, and this ran parallel to financial support provided by the national research council, which increased from roughly $14,000 in 1917-18 to $247,000 in 1938-39. In spite of this very considerable development, at the beginning of the last war we were still far behind university science in European countries and the United States. This was largely due to shortage of staff and lack of facilities.
The war brought about major developments, and by 1946 scientific research was becoming a major operation of all Canadian universities. This development was delayed in the early 1950's by the universities' financial position, but the considerable improvement in this position has resulted in a quite spectacular development in the last five years.

Atomic Energy Committee National research council support has kept pace with this development and has risen in recent years.
Industrial research in Canada, especially related to secondary industry, has suffered from some of the problems inherent in the flow of foreign capital into Canadian industry. Research frequently has been done entirely by the controlling company outside Canada. However, there has developed greater realization in recent years that Canadian companies, whether controlled from outside Canada or not, must perform research for themselves, and there has been a very satisfactory development of research in Canadian companies since the last war. Much remains to be done, but certainly the trend at the moment is an encouraging one.
The national research council has taken a considerable share in carrying on research for Canadian companies prior to the development of their own facilities, in encouraging the growth of research facilities in Canadian companies themselves and in co-operating with industrial research organizations once they come into existence. In general the development of industrial research organizations means greater awareness of problems and consequently results in more effort rather than less being necessary by the national research council in playing its part. Parallel to this development of research in Canadian industries there has, therefore, been a steady expansion of the national research council laboratories.
Government research in Canada in so far as it relates to the development of natural resources or primary products is the function of the appropriate departments concerned-agriculture, mines and technical surveys, northern affairs, and so on. This phase of research lies outside the scope of the proposed committee. In general the activity of the national research council is aimed at secondary industry rather than primary. It has, however, much broader duties than this. Its main functions consist of (1) General advice to the government on the position of science as a whole and on its relations with other activities of government. (2) It is the council's function to promote and encourage research, particularly in universities and it therefore administers a scholarship and grant-in-aid program of considerable magnitude. (3) The council in its laboratories performs research which is either direct toward secondary industry, toward fundamental science or toward fields which fall outside the specific responsibilities of the various government departments and agencies. (4) A further function of the national research council which becomes particularly important as industrial research in industry expands is that of co-ordinating 

research done by various organizations and of making sure that all interested parties are aware of what others are doing.
In order to keep pace with this, the council has developed a continually expanding group of committees for the purpose of coordinating research and various aspects of technology. At the present time the membership of such committees is over 3,300, with people drawn from the national research council, from other federal government organizations, from provincial organizations, from Canadian industry and from the universities. This committee structure has had a most important effect on Canadian scientific co-ordination.
I do not wish to go into these matters in detail since this is the function of the committee. It may, however, be worth while to mention briefly the developments which have taken place since the last committee met in 1956. As far as the national research council is concerned there have been no pronounced changes administratively. There has been, however, a noteworthy expansion in many ways. The university program has expanded greatly in order to keep up with the growth of Canadian university science, and the council's estimates for university support in science have risen from $3.0 million in 1956-57 to $9.2 million in the 1960-61 estimates. The laboratories have had a slow but steady increase. The total estimates of the council have risen from $18.6 million to $33.0 million in this period. This increase consists in part of a $6.2 million increase in university support in science. Correspondingly there has been an increase in laboratory operating estimates of $6.5 million, rising from $15 million to $21.5 million. The remaining change in estimates in the period has been brought about by an increase in capital estimates, by some increases in council revenue, and so on. In other words, during this period there has been an expansion of slightly over 200 per cent in the council's estimates for university support and of 43 per cent in the estimates for the operation of the council's laboratories.
The fundamental feature of the national research council has been its somewhat unusual governmental set-up which has developed over the past 40 years for the purpose of giving the council the flexibility and freedom which it needs to perform its functions. This flexibility is essential to the operations of the national research council, and its operations should be carried out in the future as in the past with sufficient independence to enable it to fulfil the purpose for which it was set up.
I do not intend to make a lengthy statement on Atomic Energy of Canada Limited

at this time. When the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited comes before the special committee he will not doubt wish to do so. There are, however, some general observations which I should like to make on introducing this resolution.
The government continues to support strongly the development of atomic power in this country. The special committee in 1956 in its final report hoped that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited would press forward in its work in the development of atomic power. This is being done. The estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961 for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited are $41,653,255 as against $32,092,300 for the 195960 fiscal year. This is an increase of $9,560,955 or 29.8 per cent.
The construction of the nuclear power demonstration station at Rolphton, Ontario, some 20 miles west of Chalk River on the Ottawa river, is well under way. Construction work should be finished by about the end of this year and the station should be operating a year from now. This nuclear power demonstration station has a rating of 20,000 kilowatts of electricity and will feed power into the Ontario Hydro grid system. It is being built to demonstrate the reliability of operation, the safety and the economics of the heavy water natural uranium type of reactor system. However, because the size of a reactor plant plays such an important role in the economy achieved, the cost per kilowatt-hour of power generated in this small station will be higher than for a conventional plant.
During the past four years and concurrently with the nuclear power demonstration program, the design and development of a full scale nuclear power plant has also been under way. The decision to proceed was based on the confidence of the design staff, the success of the nuclear power demonstration design, the success of the fuel development program at Chalk River, and on the realization that a full scale plant must be built and operated before the real costs of large stations can be known.
While Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is not a government department, parliament does exercise financial control over its operations. Treasury board reviews Atomic Energy of Canada Limited estimates in the same manner as it reviews those of government departments. The approved estimates are printed in the official estimates and in due course are considered and approved here in parliament.
Not many years ago, owing to security restrictions, there was very little information about atomic energy available to parliament or to the general public. Now the situation has 79951-0-247
Atomic Energy Committee changed completely. There is a very large and growing body of information available on atomic energy. Even the technical experts have, to some extent, to rely on abstracting services to keep themselves posted on what is being written. Last year Atomic Energy of Canada Limited alone issued 100 technical reports from Chalk River and had another 100 articles published in technical journals. A further 490 reports were prepared for internal use. I am informed that the Chalk River library now has 68,000 technical reports, and about 17,000 reports and micro cards are being added each year. A large number of these are being received from atomic energy organizations in other countries in exchange for the reports issued by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. For the layman, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited prepares non-technical reports and brochures and puts on exhibitions.
With all the information now available about atomic energy the government considers it useful at this time to set up a special committee as proposed in the resolution. It will give the members of the special commitee an opportunity to learn more about the activities of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and about the Canadian nuclear power program. Any questions about the program can be fully discussed and aired. The minutes of proceedings and evidence will be a valuable record. They will be very carefully studied by the atomic energy experts and those responsible for atomic energy programs in other countries; just as the accounts of similar hearings held in other atomic energy countries are read with interest here. Canada is recognized as being one of the five leading atomic energy countries in the world. In the development of nuclear power reactors using natural uranium as fuel and heavy water as the moderator we are recognized as the most advanced country. Other countries are watching our program with keen interest.
The third field of investigation for the committee is Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. In 1956 when the former committee of the house met the operations of Eldorado were under review. The committee may wish to bring up to date the information pertaining to Eldorado in relation to its mines at Port Radium and Beaverlodge, its research and development activities and its program of uranium procurement and sales. In the intervening four years since the special committee of the house met in 1956 very considerable changes have taken place which the present proposed committee may wish to examine in detail.
The committee of 1956 held a series of 12 meetings throughout May and June.
