Atomic Energy Committee of that year. A similar series may be held by this committee as it considers the three important areas under investigation, the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. In the three fields Canada has been very progressive and has established a position of prominence that has been recognized by leading countries engaged in similar activities.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER POLICY, OPERATIONS AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion as explained by the minister is that a select committee be appointed to consider the policies, operations and expenditures of the national research council, of the atomic energy corporation and of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. This is, as the minister said, a large undertaking more especially if we take into consideration the fact that we may be on the last leg of this session. It is certainly unfortunate that this motion could not have been brought forward before now.
Of course the order of procedure in committee and more particularly the order in which any one of the three crown companies will be called to appear before the committee, the number of witnesses who will be heard and the number of sittings which the committee will be able to hold are matters being left to the committee itself through the steering committee which will be appointed. However, in view of the great interest across Canada in the future and development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes, in view of the recent controversy as regards the different methods of producing nuclear power and in view also of the amount of publicity which appeared in all Canadian newspapers during the last five or six months regarding the policy and operation of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, I express the hope that the activity of these two crown companies will be studied first.
In expressing this hope I do not wish to minimize the importance of the work of the national research council. On the contrary I feel that the work of the council is growing in importance and it is very appropriate that a thorough survey of its accomplishments since 1956 be made so that hon. members of parliament and the public in general know that in this field of general research we are not lagging behind.
On the other hand, time is running short and it would be most unfortunate if before the end of the present session we were not able to have a complete survey made of atomic research and all the activities of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. In


previous parliaments committees of a similar nature were set up. The first was in 1949 and that committee was known as the committee on atomic energy. In 1950 a special committee known as the committee on the national research council was established and sat for some time and thoroughly examined the operations of that crown company. In 1953 there was a second committee on atomic energy and finally in 1956, as the minister said, another special committee was established to examine into the role of government in the field of non-military research in Canada including operations in the field of atomic energy and in the work of the national research council. I understand that at that time, four years ago, a complete review was made of the activities of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited.
We are aware that the national research council is well and efficiently operated and administered. The work of the council is of great importance to the country. Its achievements have contributed much in advancing material welfare in Canada. It contributes to the economic development of the country and the welfare of our people. We must also admit that it is an important adjunct in the defence of this country.
In 1956 we were told of the fine co-operation which existed between the council and industry. It was explained then that a free and constant flow of personnel and information is maintained between the council laboratories and industrial laboratories thus providing a most important source of information and assistance to the work of the council. In the early days of its history associated committees were established by the national research council and they have continued since. Hundreds of specialists have graciously and freely brought their knowledge and experience to bear upon the solution of many research problems. They have given their time and energy free of charge, as I have just said, and in doing this they have been a source of great strength to the council. For this they certainly deserve our most sincere thanks.
At this point I wish to extend to the officers and personnel of the national research council our congratulations and thanks for the fine work they are doing. The actual governing body of the national research council is an honorary advisory council consisting of 17 appointed members who are not government employees. They are men eminent in their fields such as university executives, deans, professors, industrialists, engineers and labour leaders. These men also bring freely to the council's deliberations their

talents, experience and achievements, things that cannot be purchased by money. These men speak with authority. They are experienced in their own field and receive no monetary remuneration. Certainly these gentlemen together with those I have mentioned earlier deserve our sincere gratitude and that of the country.
On this side of the house we feel it is appropriate for parliament to review again the activities of the national research council and to get acquainted with proposed future research developments. In fact we are of the opinion that it is highly important that members of parliament and Canadians in general be more familiar with all that is being done by the national research council to improve our technological know-how and the welfare of the nation.
During the past months there has been an increased interest across the country in some of the possibilities as well as in some of the problems for the peaceful application of atomic energy. Certainly, there is no subject which has excited more interest in recent years, and no subject about which there is still more confusion. This is readily understood. First of all, it has momentous implications for the future of mankind. Used for belligerent purposes by ambitious powers it can bring devastation to the whole world. Used for peaceful purposes it can bring untold benefits to mankind.
The most important civilian application of atomic energy is, without any doubt, the generation of nuclear power. There are also many other fields where atomic energy will play an important role in the future. How important those other uses may eventually become no one can tell.
The possibilities of using atomic energy for generating nuclear power have been the subject of a great number of articles and editorials in the newspapers of this country during the last five or six months. We have read long dissertations regarding peaceful applications of this tremendous source of energy. We have read many controversial statements on the kind of reactors that should be built for generating power, of the kind of material that should be used in such reactors, that is, natural uranium or enriched uranium, heavy water or graphite, and so forth.
We have heard of the plight of the uranium extracting industry and of the communities depending on this industry. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, most of what we have read in the newspapers has contributed to the confusion, and a great number of Canadians are also of the opinion that the present government, by its inaction, by its lack of policy, has also contributed to confuse the issue.
79951-0-247i
Atomic Energy Committee
There is no doubt that the Canadian people expect that this committee, with the help of the personnel of both or, I should say, maybe the three crown companies and the co-operation of outside witnesses, will be able to throw some light on the whole subject.
From the beginning Canada has played an important role in the development of atomic energy. Over the years our country has contributed much to the growing store of knowledge in this new and very complicated field. Canada, in many ways, has led the world in the development of atomic energy for peaceful uses. The first bombs for therapy for cancer treatment were produced at the atomic energy plant at Chalk River. I believe I am right when I say that, apart from the United States, Canada had the first reactor which was put into operation at Chalk River in 1945.
Our scientists and engineers are world leaders in natural uranium and heavy water reactors. There is no question that the NRX and NRU reactors at Chalk River are two of the finest research reactors known in the world. It is very appropriate that Canada should be taking a leading part at this time in the peaceful application of atomic energy, because many of the fundamental properties of radioactive elements and isotopes were discovered here by our own people.
It is commonly agreed that Canada must be included with those countries which are in the forefront in the development of nuclear science.
There is considerable difference of opinion as to the most suitable reactor which should be used for producing nuclear power. In the early days of Chalk River the NRX reactor was built and later the NRU. Both reactors were designed to use natural uranium and heavy water, and both were and are still considered fine reactors. First, design and feasibility studies were started early in 1954. From those studies came the outlined specifications for the demonstration power reactor, known as the NPD, nuclear power demonstrator, which is now being built, as the minister said, and I was very glad to hear it would be in operation in 1961, as previously foreseen. The nuclear fuel will be natural uranium and the moderator and primary coolant will be heavy water. This reactor was designed and is being built to produce or generate 20,000 kilowatts.
In 1955 and 1956, concurrently with the NPD program, a design study of a larger nuclear power station, with a capacity 10 times larger than the NPD, was carried out. The project has since been named the CANDU, Canadian deuterium uranium. Final
3918	HOUSE OF
Atomic Energy Committee approval to proceed with the engineering development phase of the CANDU was given in 1958, and we were told then that it would take three or four years to complete these preliminary studies and that by that time a reliable cost estimate of producing power with this reactor would be available. I hope that during the hearings of the committee we shall be able to get some definite figures, or close figures, on the probable cost of producing power in the NPD, and maybe the experts can deduce the cost of producing power in the CANDU. We were also informed that once a final decision is taken to go ahead with the construction of the CANDU it would take four of five years to have it in operation. As much as we are able to appreciate the quality of the experimental work which has been completed to date, we can say that we are well on our way and we will soon be producing nuclear power with a reactor using natural uranium and heavy water.
During the past year a certain amount of criticism has been directed toward this program and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has been blamed for having concentrated its work on one kind of reactor only, namely that of using heavy water and natural uranium. As it is-and I do not pose as an expert-I am not convinced that these criticisms are well founded. First of all, scientists and engineers who in the past have made a high reputation for themselves have started on a program which they believed was the right one. They have stuck with it, and it is undeniable that they have attained a certain amount of success. Second, we must not forget that our resources place some limit on our ability to undertake a highly diversified program. This is clearly understood, and I for one think that it is much better to do one job well than to do several jobs poorly. However, I believe I am on solid ground when I say that the majority of us here are not experts in this field of atomic energy and that only when we have heard the pros and cons will we be able to judge what is being done at the present time.
There are a great number of questions to be answered by those who will appear before this proposed committee. I am sure the committee will have full co-operation from the witnesses and in this way its work will be much easier and more satisfactory.
The present state of the uranium industry, Mr. Speaker, is not too encouraging. During the last world war, with the Belgian Congo we were the only producers of this metal. In the post-war years military demand continued to be the driving force in the worldwide search for uranium and the opening


of new mines. During the past five years our country became a major producer and in 1959 some 15,000 tons of uranium oxide, having a total value of more than $300 million, were processed in the 25 Canadian operating mines. During that same period large deposits of uranium were discovered in the United States, and during the course of the last two years it became apparent that the United States atomic energy commission, which was our most important client, might reduce its purchases of uranium from Canada.
Under contracts with Canada which were to expire March 31, 1962, and March 31, 1963, the United States atomic energy commission had the option of extending its purchases through December 31, 1966. In August, 1959 the Canadian government was informed by letter that the government of the United States would not exercise any portion of the options to purchase Canadian uranium in the post-1962 period. This was disclosed only on November 6, 1959 when the arrangements made by Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited and the Uinted States atomic energy commission and the United Kingdom atomic energy authority to allow a stretch-out of deliveries of uranium to December 31, 1966 were announced. This drastic action of our friends and clients took the floor from under the industry and from now until the end of 1966 the production of uranium in this country will gradually decline from 15,000 tons, as it was last year, to a mere few hundred tons in 1966 or 1967.
Canada unfortunately is the first country to feel the impact of the growing surplus of uranium. I must repeat that it is hard to understand the do-nothing policy of the present government during the latter part of 1958 and all of 1959 regarding our sales of uranium to the United States. The Canadian industry was developed at the urging of the United States government to satisfy the needs of that country for vital sources of uranium oxide. Even after the discovery of large reserves, fears of shortage persisted in the minds of our friends to the south, so much so that they continued to take options on the Canadian production after 1962.
It is very difficult to understand why the present government did not press further the case of the Canadian uranium industry when there was still time to negotiate some satisfactory arrangement. The United States atomic energy commission should have at least consented to exercise part of its options in the post-1962 period. No, Mr. Speaker, the government paid absolutely no attention to our requests for action. The government paid no attention to a reasonable request presented to it by Canadian Metal Mining Association

in January, 1959. One of the recommendations of the Canadian Metal Mining Association was to this effect, and I should like to quote it again:
The government of Canada do everything in its power-
That was in January, 1959.
-to have the government of the United States exercise its options on Canadian uranium production up to December 31, 1966, and give, at the earliest possible date, notification of its intention to do so.
Nothing was done officially by the Canadian government previous to August 7, 1959 when the Canadian charge d'affaires ad interim wrote to the secretary of state of the United States. At this point I wish to put the contents of these letters on the record. The letter from our charge d'affaires is dated August 7, 1959 and is addressed to the Hon. Christian A. Herter, secretary of state of the United States, Washington, D.C. It reads as follows:
Sir,
I have the honour to refer to the options for the purchase of Canadian uranium between 1962 and 1966 held by the United States atomic energy commission.
As the United States government is fully aware, the Canadian uranium industry was expanded to its present level of output primarily to supply the nuclear source material required for defence needs. The Canadian government considers it essential that the industry now be enabled to maintain itself on a sound and economic basis so that it may continue to serve those and other requirements and assumes that the United States government shares the view that this is a desirable objective. In these circumstances	and	in order	that	theCanadian uranium industry may be in a position to consider what steps	can	be taken	to bring
production and probable demand more nearly into balance my government wishes to ask whether the United States atomic energy commission will be authorized to exercise some or all of its options on Canadian production between 1962 and 1966.
In asking for an advance	clarification of	thispoint, I feel that I may	rely	upon the	close	and
mutually beneficial co-operation in this field which has long existed between our two countries.
Accept, sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
That is signed by Mr. R. A. Farquharson, charge d'affaires ad interim. The answer to the letter of the charge d'affaires is dated August 28, 1959 and is addressed to His Excellency A. D. P. Heeney, ambassador of Canada, and reads as follows:
Excellency:
I have the honour to refer to your note No. 476 of August 7, 1959 regarding the exercise of options by the United States atomic energy commission for the purchase of Canadian uranium between 1962 and 1966.
Discussions have taken place between the department of state and the atomic energy commission, and the department has been informed that the commission will not be in a position to exercise any of these options by March 31, 1961.
The government of the United States is not unmindful of the contribution made by the government of Canada in supplying uranium for the
Atomic Energy Committee
defence of the free world both during and after world war II and also for the development of peaceful uses of atomic energy.
However, the atomic energy commission is presently committed to purchase more uranium during the next three years than it requires. Considering the surplus that will be acquired during these years, the commission probably is fully committed for its uranium requirements for the next four or five years. Beyond that there are still heavy commitments, principally with domestic producers, which extend to the end of 1966.
The present position of over-commitment is due to larger increases in domestic production than anticipated. The United States atomic energy commission has already taken steps to stretch out domestic deliveries and to limit its obligations under a domestic procurement program publicly announced in 1956.
Therefore, it is with the greatest regret that the government of the United States must inform the government of Canada that it will not be in a position to exercise its options.
In view of the importance of this matter the substance of this note has been discussed with the President.
Accept, Excellency, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
These two letters, reveal, first of all, that it was the charge d'affaires who communicated with the secretary of state of the United States.

Energy is one of the keys to our national growth. On a per head basis we are one of the largest users of electricity. It is clear that in the near future the need for more extensive power resources will continue to be increasingly felt in the more populous and highly industrialized areas and provinces of this country. Ten to fifteen years from now we may have to produce twice as much energy as we are producing now.
For this reason careful consideration should be given to the possibility of developing electrical power by nuclear reactors. If we succeed, some portion-however small it is-of our domestic uranium production will be put to work in this country, thereby avoiding the large importations of coal, with the necessary adverse effect on Canada's balance of trade with the United States.
Canada has had an early start in the science of atomic energy and has been one of the pioneer countries in research for peaceful uses of this tremendous source of energy. Are we now lagging behind? I do not think

so. However, this is one of the questions which will have to be answered before this proposed committee.
Another question which will have to be answered is the following one: are we experimenting with the right kind of reactors? Again, I believe we are, but there are many people who are not of this opinion. This controversy will also have to be resolved.
Are we following up on prospective markets for uranium? This is one question which will have to be answered by the minister himself. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see this resolution before us, and trust the committee will be set up as soon as possible. I am gratified to see the wide terms of reference, particularly with regard to policy, which have been provided and which will enable the committee to engage upon the broadest possible survey of the substantive matters mentioned in the resolution.
I hope that the committee will, in fact, direct its attention to a considerable and serious discussion of the direction which our present research and development in atomic energy power is now taking. Frankly, this is a technical and complex subject, somewhat beyond me, but when I hear the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas), who is a competent professional engineer, vouchsafing his misgivings I certainly have no reason to be ashamed to say what I have said. While I
3924	HOUSE OF
Atomic Energy Committee realize that this is a subject of great technical breadth and depth yet, I think it is safe to say that I share the concern in the minds of many people as to whether we in Canada- and this is one problem which, I trust, the committee will investigate-by restricting our development and research to the heavy water type of atomic reactor are not putting all our atomic eggs into one basket, particularly in view of the fact that in the United States they have established several diffusion plants which are engaged in the production of enriched uranium.
That is an area which I trust this committee will carefully study. I say that because not only as a member of this house but as a Canadian I have a personal interest in this subject also in the sense that I come from the near north which is the source of much of our uranium production and the potential source of more and which contains the most logical place for the large quantities of hydro power required for the production of enriched uranium, namely at the proposed Peace river dam. I hope therefore the committee will give some serious thought to our policy in connection with the grave, vexatious and complex problem of atomic power production in Canada.

The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) certainly had a long contribution to make beginning on page 1700 of Hansard of that date. In any event the discussion took two and a half days and covered 63 pages of the record.
We have substantially the same motion before us today to set up a committee to consider the policy and operations of these governmental agencies and whether in our view it is wise to set up this committee for that purpose. Two of these agencies, I need hardly point out to the house, deal with the uranium industry and atomic energy generally up to the point where one of them, I believe I am right in saying, is the sole marketing agency for this commodity.
My friend the hon. member for Villeneuve speaking on this motion has already indicated the importance which has been attached in the past and which perhaps will be attached to an even greater extent in the future to research. I should like to join the hon. gentleman in the tribute he paid to the agencies in question which are referred to in this motion and to the work they have done and are doing to the skill and devotion of the officials, the officers and the workers of these three government corporations, although I think the national research council hardly qualifies as a government corporation.
Nothing could be more important than research in the development of our country and nothing could be more important than the work done in that field by these agencies of the government. Perhaps in the future a great deal more will have to be done in this field because it is becoming increasingly obvious that no country can keep up in development unless it keeps up in research. It is sad to think that at this time hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent on defence with results which to say the least are inadequate to meet the emergencies of the time when, yet compared to that amount

so little is being appropriated for the kind of research which would be of inestimable benefit to the development of our country.
I want to say a few words about the uranium industry because it is one of the matters which will undoubtedly be discussed by the committee. I think it is appropriate to consider the state of that industry at the present time before the committee is set up. No doubt the committee will go into the matter in detail and will call witnesses and experts, but this is an opportunity to give our views in the house on the subject which is covered by the words "policy and operations" of these agencies as those words appear in the motion.

speechtext: Before the hon. member goes on, in view of his indication of what he intends to say, may I say there have been some unfortunate precedents in the past of allowing extended debates on motions to set up committees. What I want to guard against -and I ask for the co-operation of the house in this-is covering here what will have to come before the committee and will be the subject of debate when the committee reports so that we do not triplicate our efforts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER POLICY, OPERATIONS AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Without regard to what may have been done on earlier occasions and which is perhaps irrelevant to your ruling I will do my best to keep within the limits Your Honour has set down.
One of the matters which undoubtedly will have to be discussed by the committee and indeed it is one of the most important subjects will be civil uses of atomic energy. Already there has been some indication in this debate as to the importance of that matter and the progress which is being made in that regard. As has already been pointed out, we in this country have taken our stand on one type of heavy water reactor. I am in no position to support or criticize that decision because it is a highly technical decision and naturally one can only be guided by the technical advice one receives on a matter of such complicated scientific importance.
In any event the decision has been made and when the committee meets no doubt 79951-0-248i
Atomic Energy Committee there will be experts brought before the committee to explain and justify that decision. One effect of the decision which has already created its own controversies in Canada among those who are on both sides qualified to have views on this matter has been to put us in a different situation in regard to the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes in the future from that which faces the United States in its development program today because they have apparently decided to proceed with the development of a different kind of reactor.
In due course we shall find out who is right, or who is wrong, or, indeed, perhaps both will be right, or conceivably even both may be wrong; but the fact remains that at the present time the divergence in policy and decision in this matter between the two countries does constitute a problem for the development of Canada in this field in so far as the use of uranium and the export of uranium are concerned because the United States will be competing with us in this field and it is a competition which is going to be, as it has already been, very difficult for us to meet. I say that because the United States has great resources at its disposal; it can offer reactors to other countries, make agreements covering the use of uranium by other countries, build reactors for them free, or on credit arrangements we cannot meet. That condition, because of the nature of the reactor in which only enriched uranium can be used-and we do not produce enriched uranium-poses a problem which we shall have to face.
It may be that one day in this country we shall have to go into the field of enriched uranium. I hope it will be one of the matters which will come before this committee, where we can get expert opinion because, as the minister knows, there are even contrary views on that subject. Perhaps we shall be able to come to some conclusion in the committee as to the cost and the desirability, or the undesirability, of proceeding at this time or in the near future with a plant for the production of enriched uranium in Canada, how much it will cost if we were to proceed with it, and all that kind of thing. Because we are going to have very great difficulties indeed in developing markets in the world for our uranium if we have to compete with the United States under contracts, the kind of which I have indicated and which would require the users of the reactors constructed by the United States to purchase a certain type of uranium which cannot be secured from Canada.
There are other limitations in our expansion in this field that we shall have to face. There is the limitation brought about in the existing individual agreements, the bilateral

Atomic Energy Committee agreements we make with other countries by international agreement. I know that these limitations are pretty strong but I think they are such, because of the nature of this commodity and the use to which it is being put in other fields than for peaceful purposes, as are valid at this time. It may, however, cause us difficulty if other exporters of uranium do not accept the same limitations in the same way as we do.
There is, of course, another difficulty facing the uranium industries immediately, a far more serious difficulty than the potential one which I have mentioned, and that is the state of the industry arising out of the refusal of the United States to take up the options in the contracts that were made between agencies of the two governments some years ago. I would think, Mr. Speaker, that this would be one of the most important matters that could be brought before this committee. It is one that should be discussed before the committee in all of its aspects, its scientific, commercial aspect, it employment aspect and, if you like, also its diplomatic aspects.
The circumstances of the original contract, the circumstances under which it was signed, I think are pretty well known to the house and, in view of the importance of this matter as a subject for discussion in the committee, I hope I may be permitted to trace the circumstances but not at any great length. It is well to remember that it is only a few years ago when we negotiated this contract with the United States in circumstances which, of course, were very different from those which existed last autumn when the question of taking up the options came up. I recall, as other hon. members will recall, that the Canadian government of that day was begged to explore with every possible rapidity to discover and to develop every ounce of uranium that could be found in this country as a product which was of vital importance for not only American but for collective defence generally. We were begged at that time to proceed with all possible speed and it was in those circumstances that a contract was signed for a five-year period, with an option to renew, at a time when there was such a shortage of uranium in the world that it was stated by our friends to the south that if they could not count on the supplies that were available in Canada collective defence would be jeopardized. So the development took place of which we are aware, and which no doubt will be considered in all of its ramifications by the committee which is being set up.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, there was no question in anybody's mind about an oversupply of uranium; there was a great fear in

a lot of people's mind about an undersupply of uranium. At that time, when this question came before a committee of this house of the type we are proposing to set up now, the preoccupation in the minds of the members of that committee was whether-and I mentioned this in the house before-we should tie up our available production of uranium for such a long period as five years. The government of that day was criticized by the opposition of the time because we had committed ourselves for five years to the shipment of all the uranium we could produce under those contracts to one source of consumption, the United States of America. If it was impossible at that time to foresee the future, did the same situation prevail a couple of years ago when the circumstances had very greatly changed?
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was discussing, not in detail but in general, the circumstances surrounding the signing of the contract between the United States and Canada with regard to the purchase of uranium. This is obviously one of the matters which the committee will wish to go into in detail because it has had an important bearing on the development and the recent slowing down of this important industry in Canada.
As I pointed out, at the time the contract was signed there was a condition of shortage in this vital defence material but it became quite clear subsequent to the signing of the contract that it was the policy of the United States government to encourage and subsidize exploration and development within its own boundaries. It was successful in doing this in terms of domestic production to the point where by 1959 United States production had risen to a total of 16,300 tons of uranium oxide per year contrasted with 15,497 tons of Canadian production. There is an interesting review of this development in the monthly review of the Bank of Nova Scotia for March, 1960, entitled "Uranium and Atomic Energy", which gives some information it would be interesting for the committee to have and which confirms what I have just said, that beginning in 1955 the United States made a big effort to increase its own production of this commodity, with the results I have just mentioned.

It was quite obvious after 1956, when this development was in full swing, that if the United States were to continue to give contracts to its domestic producers this constituted a threat to the developing Canadian industry which development was taking place at the urgent request of the United States authorities. It seemed quite obvious to me, and I have expressed this view in the House of Commons more than once in the last two years, that if the Canadian industry was to be protected, if the options were to be taken up in whole or, more likely, in part, then this would require diplomatic intervention at the highest level in both governments.
This afternoon the hon. member for Ville-neuve put on the record the report which was tabled in the house which showed that that kind of intervention did not take place, that there was merely one note sent to the United States government from the Canadian embassy calling the attention of the United States authorities to this development and its effect on the Canadian industry; a note which was sent by the charge d'affaires ad interim who was the information counsellor in the embassy and, incidentally, one of the best information officers any embassy of any government could have.
As a result the United States informed us last August that they were not going to take up any of these options. That information was not made public until late October of 1959 and as a result of that decision on the part of the United States government, a decision which I claim does not reflect the kind of industrial defence co-operation between the two countries which is so often claimed to be in effect, the industry in Canada today is in its present deteriorating position. This is one of the matters which the committee will wish to go into in great detail.
Since the United States has taken this decision-we have an even greater grievance against the United States on this point-with the disastrous effect it has had on the Canadian industry, the government of the United States, if my information is correct, has given new contracts to its own producers at a time when our production is being cut off. I, as has perhaps the minister, have read a magazine called Mining World for February, 1960 in which there is a great deal of detailed information about new contracts that has been given by the United States authorities to United States producers in this year and extending through 1966.
I claim that if we had some cause to complain about the decision last summer to ignore the options we have even greater cause to complain at subsequent activities of the United States atomic energy authorities
Atomic Energy Committee in increasing production in their own country since that time when ours is suffering from the decision taken by the United States, which has ignored a situation in which they were so interested four or five years ago when we were asked to sign this contract. That is one of the things that this committee will want to go into in great detail. We will certainly wish to get all the information we can as to what the government did or did not do to protect the Canadian industry.
I was going to go on, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the effect of this decision on some Canadian localities in terms of employment and in other respects but I bow to your ruling on this matter. No doubt that is something the committee will be able to discuss. Perhaps also we will have another opportunity to discuss it in the house later in the session. Meanwhile I should like to say in conclusion that, as the hon. member for Villeneuve has pointed out, we welcome the establishment of this committee. We asked for it three months ago and we were told then that it would be set up shortly. It is now May 16 and the committee will be set up shortly after May 16. We will co-operate in the work of that committee as best we can and we hope there will be some constructive results from it.

The minister will appreciate the situation at Uranium City. In answering a question of mine the other day and a question of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) he informed the house that two people from his department were making a survey of the situation at Uranium City. We hope that a report is received at an early date on which action can be taken to assist this community. But I would ask the minister, on behalf of the people of Uranium City and those who are affected, to give consideration, as the minister reporting for Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, to the suggestion that this company along with others should have the opportunity to exercise the right to bid on unfilled uranium contracts so that the effect of the depression now prevalent in the uranium industry will not fall unduly on the community of Uranium City.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say that I discussed the question put to me by the hon. member many, many times at the resolution stage and on second reading, and at the moment we are in committee on the first clause of this bill. However, if it will please the hon. member and if I have your permission, Mr. Chairman, may I repeat what I said on that occasion: until this trans-Canada highway is complete or close to completion, this government does not intend even to consider any further trans-Canada highway or any national plan. However, we in the department are contemplating at all times many matters including possibilities for the future, and the hon. member will probably see the wisdom of this. Nevertheless, we have no intention of considering any secondary scheme until the first is within range of completion. In saying this I am only reiterating the words of the Prime Minister which I read into the record on the resolution stage of this bill.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: If I may make a very brief reply, I should like to say that I feel the government is in error in restricting its highway activity to the limited area covered by this legislation. I believe that on the basis of resources and on the basis of employment needs it is time the government should develop a broader policy and embark on a national highway program which would include a second trans-Canada highway.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order. I think it was decided some time ago in committee that no reference could be made to a second trans-Canada highway. I was not in the chair at the time.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could tell the committee if he has received any representations from the premier of Nova Scotia or the premier of New Brunswick to the effect that the federal contribution to this trans-Canada highway plan was too low and, if so, what consideration was given to any such requests.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: That is a very broad question but according to all my knowledge I have no recollection of having received any such intimations from either one of the premiers of the two provinces mentioned, either of whom can probably appreciate that at this time it is hardly possible to change the contributory percentage under the act, this having gone on now for nearly ten years. However, we have had a request from both provinces, that the time should be extended, and that is one of the reasons we are considering clause 1 tonight, to extend it until 1963.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I should like to come back to my question and read it again. Would the minister tell the house if according to this bill the province of Quebec would be able to take part in this program. That is the first part of my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: That is a matter for the province of Quebec.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's answer when he says it is a matter for the province of Quebec to decide, but I should like to know if and when the province of Quebec chooses to put itself into the plan, is the province going to be able to recuperate what is has lost so far?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: That was the second part of the question of the hon. member for Levis, and the Chair rules it out of order.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Looking at the bill, one sees that clause 1 reads as follows:
(4) No contributions or payments shall be made under this act
(a)	after the 31st day of May, 1964 or
(b)	in respect of any construction costs that were incurred after the 31st day of December, 1963.
Now I am asking the minister a simple question: can Quebec recuperate in respect of the work done by the province between 1928 and 1949. I do remember that in 1949, when the bill was first introduced in this house, there was no time limit in respect of which the federal government could pay a province for construction work done on the trans-Canada highway, so I think my question is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I have been looking over this bill carefully and I cannot see where recuperation of expenses retroactively is relevant to the measure. I

think that is a question which could be asked, perhaps, on the estimates of the Department of Public Works.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
On that point, the bill says:
No contributions or payments shall be made under this act. ..
(b) in respect of any construction costs that were incurred after the 31st day of December, 1963.
If no contribution can be made after that date, it surely means that contributions can be made before that date in respect of construction work that was carried out before. I would therefore think that the question asked by the hon. member for Levis is relevant.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The Chair cannot give legal interpretations. I can only give procedural interpretations and the one I give is the one I think is right in the circumstances.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister if under the section which is now being amended in order to extend the time any payments have been made during the currency of the parent act to the government of any province in respect of any work done before 1949.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The answer is, yes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Then I should like to ask the minister a second question. I should like to ask him if the legislation we are now being asked to pass involves any discrimination against any one of the ten provinces of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should go back to law school. The answer to that question is, obviously, no.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Does that mean that the province of Quebec, if it chose to make an agreement, would be treated in exactly the same manner as the other provinces which already have agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. and learned member for Bonavista-Twillingate with his tremendous self-confessed ability at asking questions and making propositions and interpreting the law must realize that this is the eleventh time now that a question has been asked tonight which has been declared on previous occasions-and by yourself, Mr. Chairman-to be out of order.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I submit that my question did not relate to any other question whatsoever that was asked. My question was very simple. It was: would the government of the province of Quebec be treated, if it chose to make an agreement under this legislation now being extended, and which it is open to the government of Quebec to enter, in the
Trans-Canada Highway Act same way as the other provinces, or in a different way? That has no relation to any other question which has been asked and I feel that before we are asked to vote this money the minister should assure us that all the provinces will be treated equally and that the province of Quebec will be given exactly the same treatment as the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The Trans-Canada Highway Act was brought in under the administration of the hon. gentleman when he was the acting prime minister or the prime minister behind the scenes. I mean, the hon. member is going to write about it in a book on the life of Mackenzie King which will be coming out in published form shortly.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: This was when Mr. St. Laurent was prime minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: In short, Mr. Chairman, this is entirely out of order. We are discussing the Trans-Canada Highway Act. We speak about contributions being made under this act not after December 31, 1963. There are only nine signatories to this act at the present time. Nine of the ten provinces are signatories. We cannot conjecture in this regard. We cannot answer hypothetical questions.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Rubbish.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: My hon. friend might just as easily have asked some questions about the summit. They would have been just about as relevant. With the greatest respect, if my hon. friend would stop wiggling and confine himself to sitting still for a few minutes undisturbed and unperturbed with complete equanimity and imperturbability, I will finish my answer. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is, as usual, completely and absolutely out of order and I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, not to be intimidated by the loud talk of the hon. member.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to waste my time or yours by replying in kind to that sort of cheap performance. It is unworthy of the committee and does not need any reply. I am going to say, however, that if the minister refuses to answer the question there will be only one conclusion we can draw. The question is not hypothetical at all. I would remind the minister that when this legislation was first enacted by the house in 1949 there were agreements with no provinces and when the minister of that day introduced that legislation he did not refuse to tell the members of the committee of that day what would be in the agreements with the provinces because he had a respect for parliament and for the rights of parliament.

This legislation provides for agreements with ten provinces. It is not a hypothetical question at all to ask whether the agreement with the tenth province, if it were made, would be on the same basis as the agreements with the other nine. If the minister wants to leave the impression by refusing to answer the question that it is the intention of this government to discriminate against the province of Quebec he can go ahead and leave that impression. That is certainly the impression he is going to leave unless the hon. gentleman gives a plain and unequivocal answer to that perfectly reasonable question.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Lesage can fight his own battles.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I have one question to ask the minister. Could the hon. gentleman tell the committee whether or not the nine provinces that have agreements with the federal government under this act are treated equally?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Yes. As I explained to hon. members at the resolution stage and again on second reading, all provinces are treated in exactly the same manner so far as the Trans-Canada Highway Act is concerned. The participation of the dominion government in the act was to complete a trans-Canada highway just the same as we have a trans-Canada railway. Each province entered into exactly the same agreement except for the schedule which gave to each province the task of completing that part of the highway within its own borders. That is the purpose of it all. The province of Saskatchewan has very ably completed its task. The task is done and the province has been paid. When the other provinces will have completed their tasks in accordance with the terms of the agreements they too will be paid. For that reason all parties have been treated fairly according to the contract each and everyone of the nine signed.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's answer. I did not think it could be otherwise. I therefore fail to understand why the hon. gentleman refuses to answer the simple question as to whether, if the tenth province came into the agreement, it would be treated equitably with the other nine.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows the answer already.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No, I do not. Since the minister will not answer that fair, simple and pertinent question we can draw only one conclusion, that this government would at least consider discriminating against the province of Quebec under this act. I think that is an absolute shame.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in reply to my frienzied hon. friend who is the great authority on wheat from Assiniboia-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not even that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Medicine Hat denies him that, too. However, the hon. member for Assiniboia must surely be an authority on something. He is certainly not an authority on this act.
In reply may I simply say that the province of Quebec is able at all times to make whatever requests it wishes of us and will do so as and when it wishes. The fairness of this government in its treatment of the provinces is best illustrated by the manner in which the university grants were disposed of recently by this house. There is no province with which the Diefenbaker government has better or more amicable relations than with the distinguished government of the province of Quebec.
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that if it were within my purview to answer these hypothetical questions which you have declared to be out of order as did the chairman, I would be most delighted to do so but it would be quite improper for me even to attempt to do so. I therefore am going to maintain the determination I made at the beginning of this debate and my hon. friends may go on to make all the imputations and insults they like but nevertheless I reiterate that I am being fair with the committee in refusing to try to give accurate answers to completely hypothetical questions regarding a situation that does not exist except in the imagination of some of the hon. members.
I have been told that one should stick to the bill and I am doing my best in this respect. I will strive to stick to section 1 of this bill which asks for an extension of the time till 1963. That is all that is before the committee at the present time.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understood the minister to say that the matter before the committee is the extension of the act to 1963. We are now in 1960.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Do we understand that if Quebec comes into the plan between now and 1963 they will have a full share of the federal contribution that all the provinces heretofore had?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: In my humble opinion there is no retroactive provision in this bill. Accordingly, I think questions in this regard are not relevant to clause 1. I hope I will not have to remind hon. members about this again.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: We are witnessing Mr. Lesage's puppet show.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to put another question to the minister. Up till now was there any request by the provincial government of Quebec to participate in the plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, there has been no request. I of course resent very much the suggestion which only the hon. member for Assiniboia would have the effrontery to make, that there has been any discrimination. This government is guilty of no discrimination at any time to any province including the province of Quebec and not even the hon. member for Levis would suggest that.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: To keep the record straight, I did not suggest there was discrimination. I assume the minister would agree that if Quebec wanted to come in under the act that province would receive equitable treatment. The minister would not say. Why he would not, I cannot imagine unless perhaps he wishes to discriminate against Quebec-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: A false innuendo.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: -if and when that province should be desirous of coming in under the act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: We want Fisher; we want Fisher.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I feel strongly that the people of Quebec should be getting the same benefits under this act that are accruing to the citizens of other provinces.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Stick to wheat.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The reason they are not getting these benefits has been a decision of their provincial government.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The government of Quebec does not need the hon. member's help to make a decision either.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I trust that if and when Quebec comes under the provisions of this act this government will not even consider discriminating against that province.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would draw Your Honour's attention to the explanatory note in section 1 of this act, which says:
This amendment would extend for three years the period during which contributions or payments may be made to the provinces-
It does not say the nine provinces, it says "to the provinces" and clearly implies all of them. I continue:
Trans-Canada Highway Act -under the act and would prolong for three years the period in respect of which constructor costs may be incurred under this act.
I have been a member of this house somewhat longer than the Minister of Public Works and I have been observing it for 20 years, and I have never before known any minister of the crown, in dealing with legislation on a matter having to do with agreements that are to be made with another government, refusing to tell us what authority he was asking for and what authority he was getting from parliament to do these things.
The minister seems to have forgotten that he is responsible to parliament; that he is the servant of this house, not its master, and that he is asking this parliament to continue for three more years the authority which was given to the government to make agreements, or to continue agreements, with the provinces of Canada, including the province of Quebec. Surely before we are asked to extend the period of time and to vote a very large sum of money the parliament of Canada, the representatives of the taxpayers, are entitled to know precisely the terms and conditions under which this money can be spent. That is all we are asking for, Mr. Chairman.
I would draw your attention to the fact that the explanatory note to this clause says precisely that. There can be no question that the government is asking for three more years in which it may be possible to reach agreement with the government of Quebec in a co-operative effort to build a trans-Canada highway through that province. That is not hypothetical; it is an actual question, what kind of agreement the government would make. Parliament never intended that the government should make one kind of agreement with one province and another kind of agreement with another province. All we are seeking to find out is whether the government does in fact intend to treat the government of Quebec in the same way as it has treated the governments of the other nine provinces, and we cannot get any answer. The only conclusion we can draw is the conclusion drawn by the hon. member for Assiniboia that the government intends, if Quebec does try to come in, to shortchange it.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: A foul innuendo.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

speechtext:
May I know from the
minister whether the province of Nova Scotia, which signed an agreement in 1952, was able to secure reimbursement from the government for the actual cost of the construction that was undertaken before and which was made part of the trans-Canada highway?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I have no idea, Mr. Chairman. We are considering clause 1 of this bill.

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. Surely when we are being asked to extend this legislation we are entitled to know what has already happened under the legislation we are being asked to extend. speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Obviously, the Mutt and Jeff team over there, sent down by the-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The new plumber of the House of Commons should withdraw that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I am very proud of being that, the Minister of Public Works, and enjoy it thoroughly. I think that the two speakeasies over there should confine themselves to clause 1 of this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order. I hope the minister will address himself to clause 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I thought clause 1 had passed, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Again, Mr. Chairman, I will amend my remarks and say, let these two worthy members address themselves to clause 1 of the bill.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, am I out of order in asking the minister the simple question whether the bill is constitutional in all respects? As members of parliament I think we are entitled not to be brushed aside by a plumber.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, according to what rule of the house does the minister not answer my question? It is a very simple and at the same time very important one, and the minister knows it. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know why the minister does not want to answer that question. I refer to Hansard of April 28 when he said, "Does the hon. member know that a provincial election has been called in Quebec on the twenty second of June?" That is the second time we have received-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: -that kind of answer. Does it mean that when we are going to have a provincial election in Canada-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: -we are not entitled to receive answers to our questions?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: You are getting funnier by the minute.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: You know the reputation you have.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
